message.content: tell me about the project

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

addedBlocks:
## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

attachment.content:
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

=== README ===
# research

Research on model weights, layers, and activations — running locally on a
Snapdragon X (Windows ARM64) laptop.

## Layout

```
src/research/     importable package
  paths.py        canonical project paths
  models.py       weights / layers / activations access
notebooks/        exploratory notebooks
scripts/          runnable entry points
models/           HF weight cache (gitignored, large)
results/<model>/  every output, split per model
data/raw|interim|processed/    gitignored contents, tracked shape
tests/            pytest suite
docs/             findings and methodology
```

## Setup

This project runs on **native ARM64 Python 3.13** — not the emulated x64 build.
`torch` must come from the PyTorch index; PyPI ships no `win_arm64` wheel, and
`pyproject.toml` already routes `torch` to that index for uv.

The environment is uv-managed and pinned by `uv.lock`. One command builds it:

```bash
uv sync --extra dev
```

That creates `.venv`, installs the locked versions, and installs `research`
itself editable, so `import research` works everywhere. `uv` resolves a bare
`3.13` to the **ARM64** interpreter, not the x64 one also on this machine.

To rebuild the environment from scratch:

```bash
uv venv .venv --clear --python 3.13
```

`uv sync` takes about **7 seconds** on NTFS, because uv hardlinks from its cache
instead of copying. (On the exFAT volume this project used to live on, which
supports neither symlinks nor hardlinks, the same command took **19 minutes**.
If it is ever slow again, check the filesystem first.)

## Where results go

Every output lands in `results/`, in a subfolder named for the model, so results
are never mixed between models:

```python
MODEL_ID = "gpt2"
OUT = paths.results_dir(MODEL_ID)        # results/gpt2/  (created for you)
fig.savefig(OUT / "residual-norm-by-depth.png", dpi=150)
```

The id is slugged, so `google/gemma-3-1b-it` becomes `results/google_gemma-3-1b-it/`
and `gemma3:1b` becomes `results/gemma3_1b/`. Always derive the folder from
`MODEL_ID` rather than typing it — that is what stops a model switch from
overwriting another model's results.

Results are tracked in git (they are the deliverable); tensors and checkpoints
under `results/` are gitignored.

## Working in Jupyter

Coding happens in notebooks. Launch JupyterLab from the project root:

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python -m jupyterlab
```

- **Select the `Python (research ARM64)` kernel.** The `python3` kernel on this
  machine is an emulated x64 interpreter with no PyTorch — it will fail on
  `import torch`.
- `notebooks/00-getting-started.ipynb` walks the whole workflow end to end:
  loading a model, listing layers, reading weights, capturing activations, and
  inspecting models too large for RAM. Outputs are kept in that one, so it reads
  as documentation without being run.
- `notebooks/01-beam-search.ipynb` finds the highest-probability continuations of
  a prompt by beam search, with every selection decision traced. **Not yet run** —
  it writes `results/<model>/`, and its findings belong in `docs/beam-search.md`.
- `notebooks/02-beam-search-across-architectures.ipynb` runs that same search over
  four models spanning three mechanism families. **Not yet run** — its findings
  belong in `docs/beam-search-across-architectures.md`.
- `notebooks/_template.ipynb` is the starting point for new work.
- Every notebook opens with `import research` — before `transformers` — so the
  model cache is pinned to D:.
- **Notebooks are self-sufficient**: the logic a notebook demonstrates lives in
  the notebook, and duplication between notebooks is accepted. `src/research/`
  holds infrastructure (paths, the cache guard, weight access), not analysis
  logic. Cells carrying an algorithm are tagged so the tests can execute the
  notebook's own code — see `tests/test_beam.py`.

If the kernel is missing from the launcher, register it:

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python -m ipykernel install --user --name research --display-name "Python (research ARM64)"
```

## Checks

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python -m pytest -m "not slow"
```

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python -m ruff check .
```

## Where models are downloaded

All weights land in `models/` at the project root, never in the default Hugging
Face cache under your user profile (`~/.cache/huggingface`).
`research/__init__.py` sets `HF_HUB_CACHE` to do this, which means **import
`research` before `transformers`**.

`models/` is a **directory junction onto D:** — physically `D:/research/models`,
so ~25 GB of weights stay off the system drive while the code still just sees
`<project>/models`. Recreate it with
`mklink /J C:\research\models D:\research\models`, and don't delete
`D:/research/models`: it is the real folder, not a copy.

That drive is slow to read, so a model you will load more than once can be
**staged** onto the fast volume:

```python
model, tok = models.load("Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B", stage=True)
```

This copies that one model into `.model-cache/` and loads from there. The slot
holds **exactly one model** — staging another evicts the first — so it cannot
grow into a second copy of `models/`. Measured on Qwen3-1.7B: 105.7 s loading
direct from D:, 120.7 s on the staging run, then 16.1 s every load afterwards.
It is a net loss for a single one-off load, and worth most at bfloat16, where
the weights stay memory-mapped and the file's volume serves every page fault.
`models.staged_model()` reports what is resident; `models.clear_stage()` empties it.

```python
import research                      # pins the cache - must come first
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")   # -> C:/research/models
```

Or skip the ordering concern entirely by using the helper:

```python
from research import models
model, tok = models.load("gpt2")
```

This is **enforced**, not merely defaulted. Loading a model from anywhere
else - including the pre-existing HF cache in your user profile on C: -
raises `ExternalModelError`:

```python
models.load(profile_cache / 'models--Qwen--Qwen3-0.6B')
# ExternalModelError: C:/Users/.../models--Qwen--Qwen3-0.6B is outside
#                     C:/research/models
```

Re-download by repo id instead. `models/` is gitignored; put `HF_TOKEN` in
`.env` for gated repos such as Gemma.

## Accessing weights and layers

```python
from research import models

model, tok = models.load("gpt2")           # cached under models/

# Every parameterised submodule, with shapes
for row in models.layer_table(model)[:5]:
    print(row["name"], row["class"], row["params"], row["shapes"])

# One weight tensor by dotted name
w = models.weight(model, "transformer.h.0.attn.c_attn.weight")   # (768, 2304)

# Activations, via forward hooks
import torch
with models.capture(model, ["transformer.h.0", "transformer.ln_f"]) as acts:
    with torch.no_grad():
        model(**tok("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt"))
acts["transformer.h.0"].shape        # (1, 5, 768)
```

Inspect weights **without loading the model** — works on files larger than RAM,
since nothing is materialised:

```python
t = models.raw_tensors("models/models--gpt2/snapshots/<hash>")
t["h.0.attn.c_attn.weight"]          # ((768, 2304), 'F32', 'model.safetensors')
one = models.read_tensor(path, "h.0.attn.c_attn.weight")
```

Read the quantised GGUF weights Ollama already has on disk, to compare against
the original safetensors:

```python
blob = models.ollama_blob("gemma3:1b")
models.gguf_tensors(blob)[:3]
```

## Known limits on this machine

- **16 GB unified RAM, CPU only.** A model at float32 needs ~4 bytes/param, so
  the practical ceiling for a full torch load is roughly **1–3 B parameters**.
  Use `dtype=torch.bfloat16` to halve that when a model would not otherwise fit.
- **`datasets`, `transformer_lens`, and `nnsight` cannot be installed.** All
  three require `pyarrow`, which ships no `win_arm64` wheel. `models.capture()`
  covers the hook-based workflow those libraries wrap.
- See [docs/arm64-python-stack.md](docs/arm64-python-stack.md) for the full
  wheel-availability survey, and
  [docs/local-llm-on-snapdragon-x.md](docs/local-llm-on-snapdragon-x.md) for
  measured inference throughput.

## Conventions

- Notebooks are self-sufficient; copying a cell between them is fine. Only
  infrastructure — paths, the HF cache guard, weight access — belongs in
  `src/research/`.
- Resolve paths via `research.paths`, never with relative strings.
- Secrets live in `.env` (gitignored); document new keys in `.env.example`.

----- docs/arm64-python-stack.md
# Python ML stack on Windows ARM64 — what installs and what does not

Surveyed 2026-08-21 against PyPI and the PyTorch index, on Snapdragon X /
Windows 11 ARM64. Every claim below was checked by querying the package index
for `win_arm64` wheels, not from memory.

## The interpreter trap

`python` on this machine's PATH was **Python 3.13.7 (AMD64)** — an x64 build
running under emulation, despite `platform.machine()` reporting `ARM64`. The
only reliable check is `sys.version`, which names the build architecture:

```python
import sys; print(sys.version)
# ...[MSC v.1944 64 bit (ARM64)]   <- native
# ...[MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]   <- emulated
```

Version choice is forced, and the window is narrow:

| Interpreter | torch available? |
|---|---|
| 3.14 ARM64 (was the machine default) | **No** — no cp314 `win_arm64` wheel exists |
| 3.13 x64 | Yes, torch 2.13.0 — but every op runs emulated |
| **3.13 ARM64** | **Yes, torch 2.9.1+cpu — native. This is the one to use.** |
----- docs/candidate-models-7b-2026.md
# Four ~7B open-weight models from 2026, with four different architectures

Compiled 2026-08-21. Selected for **architectural diversity** rather than
benchmark scores: the point is that comparing them exercises genuinely
different mechanisms, not four variations of the same decoder stack.

## The shortlist

| Model | Released | Params | Architecture family | Context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Falcon-H1R 7B** (TII) | 5 Jan 2026 | 7B dense | Hybrid: attention + Mamba-2 SSM interleaved | 256K |
| **Qwen3.5-9B** (Alibaba) | 2 Mar 2026 | 9B dense | Dense transformer + GQA (the baseline) | 262K |
| **Gemma 4 E4B** (Google) | 2 Apr 2026 | 8B total / 4.5B effective | MatFormer nesting + Per-Layer Embeddings | 128K |
| **LFM2.5-8B-A1B** (Liquid AI) | 28 May 2026 | 8.3B total / 1.5B active | Sparse MoE on the LFM2 conv-hybrid backbone | 128K |

> **Correction (2026-08-21):** the "Qwen3.5-9B = dense transformer" claim below
> came from a release-tracker summary and is **wrong**. Its weights carry
> `linear_attn.A_log` / `dt_bias` state-space parameters in every decoder layer,
> putting it in the same mechanism family as Falcon-H1R. The set therefore spans
> three distinct architecture families, not four. Measured evidence in

# Python ML stack on Windows ARM64 — what installs and what does not

Surveyed 2026-08-21 against PyPI and the PyTorch index, on Snapdragon X /
Windows 11 ARM64. Every claim below was checked by querying the package index
for `win_arm64` wheels, not from memory.

## The interpreter trap

`python` on this machine's PATH was **Python 3.13.7 (AMD64)** — an x64 build
running under emulation, despite `platform.machine()` reporting `ARM64`. The
only reliable check is `sys.version`, which names the build architecture:

```python
import sys; print(sys.version)
# ...[MSC v.1944 64 bit (ARM64)]   <- native
# ...[MSC v.1944 64 bit (AMD64)]   <- emulated
```

Version choice is forced, and the window is narrow:

| Interpreter | torch available? |
|---|---|
| 3.14 ARM64 (was the machine default) | **No** — no cp314 `win_arm64` wheel exists |
| 3.13 x64 | Yes, torch 2.13.0 — but every op runs emulated |
| **3.13 ARM64** | **Yes, torch 2.9.1+cpu — native. This is the one to use.** |

# Four ~7B open-weight models from 2026, with four different architectures

Compiled 2026-08-21. Selected for **architectural diversity** rather than
benchmark scores: the point is that comparing them exercises genuinely
different mechanisms, not four variations of the same decoder stack.

## The shortlist

| Model | Released | Params | Architecture family | Context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Falcon-H1R 7B** (TII) | 5 Jan 2026 | 7B dense | Hybrid: attention + Mamba-2 SSM interleaved | 256K |
| **Qwen3.5-9B** (Alibaba) | 2 Mar 2026 | 9B dense | Dense transformer + GQA (the baseline) | 262K |
| **Gemma 4 E4B** (Google) | 2 Apr 2026 | 8B total / 4.5B effective | MatFormer nesting + Per-Layer Embeddings | 128K |
| **LFM2.5-8B-A1B** (Liquid AI) | 28 May 2026 | 8.3B total / 1.5B active | Sparse MoE on the LFM2 conv-hybrid backbone | 128K |

> **Correction (2026-08-21):** the "Qwen3.5-9B = dense transformer" claim below
> came from a release-tracker summary and is **wrong**. Its weights carry
> `linear_attn.A_log` / `dt_bias` state-space parameters in every decoder layer,
> putting it in the same mechanism family as Falcon-H1R. The set therefore spans
> three distinct architecture families, not four. Measured evidence in
> [weight-layout-comparison.md](weight-layout-comparison.md).

## What it is

`C:\research` is a **local model-internals research project** — the deliverable is findings, not an app. It studies open-weight LLM weights, layers, and activations on a Snapdragon X / Windows 11 ARM64 laptop (16 GB unified RAM, **CPU only**, no GPU).

## Shape of the repo

| Path | Role |
|---|---|
| `src/research/` | Infrastructure *only* — `paths.py` (canonical paths, `results_dir()` slugging) and `models.py` (loading, staging, layer tables, `capture()` hooks, `raw_tensors()` header reads) |
| `notebooks/` | The working surface — where analysis actually happens |
| `docs/` | Where findings get written up (4 docs so far) |
| `results/<model>/` | Per-model outputs, tracked in git |
| `scripts/compare_architectures.py` | Reads safetensors headers off the Hub without downloading |
| `tests/` | pytest, including tests that `exec` tagged notebook cells |

## The governing constraints

Most of the design is downstream of three hardware facts:

1. **ARM64 Python 3.13 only.** `torch==2.9.1` comes from the PyTorch index via `[tool.uv.sources]`; `pip install -e .` would fail. `pyarrow` has no `win_arm64` wheel, which transitively kills `datasets`, `transformer_lens`, and `nnsight` — hence the hand-rolled `models.capture()`.
2. **~4 bytes/param at float32 caps a full load near 1–3 B params.** Anything bigger gets inspected via safetensors headers instead of materialised.
3. **Weights live on D:** — `models/` is a junction onto `D:/research/models`, pinned by forcing `HF_HUB_CACHE` in `research/__init__.py`. That's why every notebook opens with `import research` before `transformers`, and why `models.load(..., stage=True)` exists (D: reads are slow: 105.7 s → 16.1 s after staging).

## Two strong conventions worth knowing

- **Model-agnostic code.** `MODEL_ID` is the single line that changes. No literal module paths (`transformer.h.0` vs `model.layers.N`), no hard-coded layer/head/vocab counts — use `models.block_names()` / `models.find()`.
- **Self-sufficient notebooks.** Duplication between notebooks is *deliberate*, not a defect. Algorithm cells are tagged (`beam-search-implementation`) so `tests/test_beam.py` runs the notebook's own code out of the `.ipynb` — that's what keeps copy-paste from costing coverage.

## Where the work stands

Committed history runs: scaffold → ARM64 stack survey → HF cache pinning → weights/layers/activations access → a shortlist of four ~7B 2026 models (Falcon-H1R, Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 E4B, LFM2.5-8B-A1B) → a header-only weight-layout comparison of all four. One nice detail in `docs/candidate-models-7b-2026.md`: a published claim that Qwen3.5-9B is a dense transformer was **corrected by measurement** — its weights carry `linear_attn.A_log` / `dt_bias`, so the set spans three mechanism families, not four.

There's a **substantial uncommitted body of work** on top:

- `notebooks/01-beam-search.ipynb` — memory-efficient beam search with a fully traced search tree (parent lineage, per-step survival, greedy baseline).
- `notebooks/02-beam-search-across-architectures.ipynb` — the same search over four *small* stand-ins (gpt2, LFM2-1.2B, Falcon-H1-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B), because the real shortlist needs 28–34 GiB at float32.

# Four ~7B open-weight models from 2026, with four different architectures

Compiled 2026-08-21. Selected for **architectural diversity** rather than
benchmark scores: the point is that comparing them exercises genuinely
different mechanisms, not four variations of the same decoder stack.

## The shortlist

| Model | Released | Params | Architecture family | Context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Falcon-H1R 7B** (TII) | 5 Jan 2026 | 7B dense | Hybrid: attention + Mamba-2 SSM interleaved | 256K |
| **Qwen3.5-9B** (Alibaba) | 2 Mar 2026 | 9B dense | Dense transformer + GQA (the baseline) | 262K |
| **Gemma 4 E4B** (Google) | 2 Apr 2026 | 8B total / 4.5B effective | MatFormer nesting + Per-Layer Embeddings | 128K |
| **LFM2.5-8B-A1B** (Liquid AI) | 28 May 2026 | 8.3B total / 1.5B active | Sparse MoE on the LFM2 conv-hybrid backbone | 128K |

> **Correction (2026-08-21):** the "Qwen3.5-9B = dense transformer" claim below
> came from a release-tracker summary and is **wrong**. Its weights carry
> `linear_attn.A_log` / `dt_bias` state-space parameters in every decoder layer,
> putting it in the same mechanism family as Falcon-H1R. The set therefore spans
> three distinct architecture families, not four. Measured evidence in
> [weight-layout-comparison.md](weight-layout-comparison.md).

## All four are autoregressive — verified

Confirmed against vendor documentation, not assumed:

| Model | Decoder-only, next-token AR? | Source of the claim |
|---|---|---|
| Falcon-H1R 7B | Yes | described as a decoder-only LLM; Mamba-2 layers are causal recurrences |
| Qwen3.5-9B | Yes | conventional dense causal decoder |
| Gemma 4 E4B | Yes | "Gemma 4 models follow a decoder-only Transformer architecture" |
| LFM2.5-8B-A1B | Yes | "retains a decoder-only LFM2 backbone ... decoder-only autoregressive" |

The distinction worth holding onto: **architecture family is orthogonal to the
generation objective.** SSM layers, MoE routing, per-layer embeddings and short
convolutions all change *how a token is computed*; none of them change the fact
that tokens are produced one at a time, left to right, each conditioned on its
predecessors. Every one of these is trained on next-token prediction.

Two things that look like exceptions but are not:

- **Gemma 4 ships a draft model for speculative decoding.** That is a decoding
  optimisation — the draft proposes tokens the main model verifies — and the
  output distribution is unchanged. Still autoregressive.
- **Mamba/SSM layers are recurrent, not attentional.** Recurrence is if anything
  *more* strictly sequential than attention. Still autoregressive.

The genuine non-autoregressive alternative is a **diffusion language model**,
which denoises a whole sequence in parallel over several passes rather than
extending it token by token. None of the four are of that kind. If a non-AR
comparison is ever wanted, that is the family to look in — and it would need
sourcing separately, as none was surveyed here.

## Why each one is architecturally distinct

**Falcon-H1R 7B** interleaves standard transformer attention layers with Mamba-2
state-space layers in one stack. The SSM layers carry a fixed-size recurrent
state instead of a growing KV cache, which is what buys the 256K context. For
weight-level work this is the interesting one: the parameter *shapes* in an SSM
layer (state-transition, input/output projections, per-channel decay) have no
analogue in an attention block.

**Qwen3.5-9B** is the control. A conventional dense decoder with grouped-query
attention and native vision. Include it precisely because it is ordinary — it is
the reference every other measurement is read against.

**Gemma 4 E4B** carries 8B total parameters but activates ~4.5B, and does so by a
mechanism unlike MoE routing. Per-Layer Embeddings feed each decoder layer its
own auxiliary embedding signal rather than relying only on the input embedding,
and MatFormer trains nested sub-models inside one checkpoint. So "how many
parameters does this model have" has three different defensible answers, which
makes it a good stress test for any parameter-counting code.

**LFM2.5-8B-A1B** is sparse MoE — 8.3B total, ~1.5B active per token — built on
Liquid AI's LFM2 backbone rather than a plain transformer. Routing means the
per-token compute and the parameter count diverge sharply, and expert weights
are a distinct tensor layout from dense FFN weights.

## Feasibility on this machine

Established earlier: 16 GB unified RAM, CPU only. That splits cleanly.

| Task | Feasible? |
|---|---|
| `raw_tensors()` / `read_tensor()` — shapes, dtypes, per-tensor stats | **Yes, all four.** Nothing is materialised, so size does not matter. |
| Quantised inference via Ollama (Q4, ~5 GB) | **Yes**, where a GGUF exists — expect ~5 tok/s. |
| Full `torch` load for activations / hooks | **No.** 7B at float32 is 28 GB; bfloat16 is ~14 GB against 15.61 GB total. |

So these four are usable for **weight-level** research immediately, and for
activation-level work only via their smaller siblings (Qwen3.5-2B, Gemma 4 E2B).

## Warning for the model-agnostic code

This shortlist is a real test of the "changing model is a text change" rule, and
parts of it will fail — by design:

- `models.blocks()` finds the block stack structurally, so it should hold across
  all four.
- `models.find(model, "attn|self_attn")` will return **fewer matches than there
  are blocks** on Falcon-H1R (only some layers are attention) and may return
  nothing useful on LFM2.5's conv blocks. That is the correct outcome — a loud
  mismatch rather than silently analysing the wrong tensors.
- Any code assuming `n_layers == len(attention_layers)` breaks on Falcon-H1R.
- Parameter-count code must decide explicitly between total, active, and
  effective parameters. Gemma 4 E4B and LFM2.5-8B-A1B disagree on all three.

## Verification status

Release dates, parameter counts, and architecture claims were taken from the
sources below rather than from model memory. **Licences were not individually
verified** — Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 are reported as Apache-2.0; Falcon-H1R and
LFM2.5 ship under their vendors' own licences and should be checked before any
commercial use.

Two candidates were considered and rejected: **Mamba-3** (Apache-2.0,
17 Mar 2026) is a genuine pure-SSM architecture but published checkpoints stop
around 1.5B, so it does not meet the ~7B bar; **Nemotron 3 Nano** is a
Mamba-2/attention MoE hybrid but is 31.6B total (3B active), too large here.

## Key Architectural Trends

By mid-2026, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture has become the dominant design pattern across every serious open-weight release. A Mixture-of-Experts architecture is a neural network design that combines multiple specialized sub-models the "experts" and a gating network that decides which experts to use for a given input.

## Notable 2026 Models

Several significant models have emerged in 2026:

- **GLM-5.2**: Released on June 13, 2026, GLM-5.2 is a 744B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with approximately 40B active per token, a usable 1M-token context window, and MIT-licensed weights.

- **DeepSeek V4**: DeepSeek-V4 is DeepSeek's latest next-generation open-weight mixture-of-experts model family with 1M input context window, including Pro and Flash variants with long-context support and agent-oriented post-training.

- **Qwen Series**: Qwen3.5/3.6 Series is a family of open-weight foundation models developed by Alibaba Cloud, built on a hybrid architecture combining Gated Delta Networks (linear attention) with sparse mixture-of-experts routing.

- **Mistral Updates**: Mistral confirmed in early July 2026 that a larger "fat but sparse" MoE family entered early access with research and government partners, with no public parameter count, benchmarks, or ship date yet.

For the specific parameter ranges you mentioned, medium models (7B-15B) often provide the best balance for most applications, though the search results show that most new 2026 releases have shifted toward larger MoE models with higher active parameters rather than dense models in the 7B-15B range.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Zyphra ZAYA1-8B architecture and its Compressed Convolutional Attention:

## Overview

ZAYA1-8B is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model that matches or exceeds substantially larger open-weight models on complex reasoning, mathematics, and coding tasks while using fewer than one billion active parameters.

## Compressed Convolutional Attention (CCA)

ZAYA1-8B uses Compressed Convolutional Attention (CCA), a FLOP- and memory-efficient attention variant that performs sequence mixing in a compressed latent space. This results in an 8x reduction in KV-cache size compared to full multi-head attention, enabling more efficient long-context reasoning.

CCA has several core components including low-rank projections that reduce compute and memory, sequence-mixing convolutions that act as lightweight preconditioners before attention, a time delay applied to half of the value heads, and skip connections and normalization with head-wise temperature applied to the keys.

## Additional Architectural Innovations

ZAYA1-8B builds on Zyphra's MoE++ architecture, with three main changes relative to standard transformer MoE designs. Beyond CCA, the model also features a ZAYA1 router, which replaces the standard linear MoE router with a multi-layer MLP-based design, substantially increasing its expressiveness.

The model combines CCA with a 4:1 grouped-query attention layout, where 8 query heads share 2 key/value heads.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about NVIDIA Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion 8B:

## Architecture Overview

Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion is a tri-mode language model that supports both AR (autoregressive) decoding and diffusion-based parallel decoding by simply switching the attention pattern of the same model during inference. The synergy between these two modes enables a third mode, called self-speculation: the same model performs diffusion-based parallel drafting and AR verification with shared KV cache, achieving high acceptance lengths and decoding efficiency.

## Technical Specifications

The language decoder has 34 layers, 4096 hidden dimensions, and 14336 intermediate dimensions. The authors train both autoregressive and diffusion objectives together with a weighted loss, with the two objectives being complementary rather than competing.

## Open Weights & Licensing

Weights are available at NVIDIA's Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion collection under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License, which permits commercial use. The weights (3B, 8B, and 14B, with base, instruct, and vision-language variants) are posted to the NVIDIA collection on Hugging Face.

## Performance

The 8B model decodes 6x more tokens per forward pass than Qwen3-8B at comparable accuracy, giving 4x throughput on SPEED-Bench with SGLang on a GB200.

I've found detailed information about Meta's Muse Glimmer from August 2026. Here's what the search results show:

## Model Overview
On August 10, 2026, Meta Superintelligence Labs open-sourced Muse Glimmer — a 30-billion-parameter, multimodal, dense model — under Apache 2.0.

## Architecture Details
Glimmer activates all 30B parameters on every token (unlike mixture-of-experts models that route through a small subset), a deliberate architecture choice suited to running whole on a single consumer GPU. The core language model is a dense causal transformer with a hidden dimension of 6,656 across 52 layers. It uses grouped query attention (GQA) with a 16:1 ratio, 32 query heads and just 2 key-value heads.

## Vision Component
For vision, Meta included a frozen 1.8B parameter ViT-G/14 encoder 50 layers wide, 1536 dimensions, with 14x14 patch size. It can process up to 4,096 visual tokens per image, enabling rich multimodal understanding of screenshots, charts, and documents.

## Context and Tokenization
Context length is 131,072+, vocabulary is 202,048 tokens, and the knowledge cutoff is January 4, 2026. The vocabulary is large at 202,048 tokens: 200,000 from BPE tokenization plus 2,048 special tokens reserved for tool schemas, reasoning markers, and system control.

## Use Cases
It's explicitly built for "always-on local agent" use cases — function calling, local coding, long tool-use sessions, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation — rather than optimized primarily for chat quality.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about IBM Granite 4 with the Mamba-2 hybrid architecture:

## Overview

IBM Granite 4.0 is the fourth generation of IBM's Granite family of open-weight enterprise large language models, released on October 2, 2025.

## Architecture

The headline innovation is a hybrid architecture that replaces most of the self-attention layers found in conventional Transformers with Mamba-2 state-space-model layers, retaining only a minority of attention blocks and adding mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing in some variants. More specifically, in the H variants, layers alternate between Mamba-2 state-space blocks and conventional Transformer attention blocks in a roughly 9-to-1 ratio, meaning the large majority of layers are Mamba-2 and only a small fraction use self-attention.

## 7B Model Specifications

For smaller-scale or edge deployments, Granite 4.0 offers the Granite-4.0-H-Tiny, a 7B-parameter hybrid with 1B active parameters. The architecture leverages Mamba-2, superimposed with a softmax attention for enhanced expressiveness, with no positional encoding for better length generalization.

## Performance Benefits

IBM claims the hybrid design cuts memory use by more than 70 percent for long-context and concurrent-session inference while preserving instruction-following and tool-use quality.

## Licensing

The models are released by IBM as open weights under the Apache 2.0 license and were the first open model family covered by an accredited ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI management systems.

**Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-8B** is the one I'd most want you to take. Your own `docs/candidate-models-7b-2026.md` closes by noting that a genuine non-autoregressive comparison would need a diffusion LM and that "none was surveyed here." **ZAYA1-8B** has the most unusual weight layout in the list. Compressed Convolutional Attention does sequence mixing in a compressed latent space with convolutions as preconditioners, an 8× KV-cache reduction, plus a time delay on half the value heads. The router is an MLP rather than the standard linear layer, and there's learned residual scaling. The 8.4B/760M split is an **11:1 sparsity ratio** — much more extreme than LFM2.5's 5.5:1, which makes it a sharper stress test for the total-vs-active parameter counting you already flagged as a hazard.

The architecture has 24 layers, of which 18 are double-gated short-convolution blocks based on the lab's proprietary LIV design, and 6 are GQA layers (Grouped Query Attention, an efficient form of attention that shares keys across multiple heads to reduce memory consumption). 8B indicates the total parameters (8.3 billion to be precise), while A1B stands for "active 1B", meaning the number of parameters actually computed at each pass. The model has 8.3B total parameters, 1.5B active per token (MoE with 32 experts, 4 active).

## Additional Features

The context length is 131,072 tokens (128K), and the vocabulary was doubled, growing from 65,536 to 128,000 tokens. LFM2.5-8B-A1B is a reasoning-only model, producing an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

## Overview

LFM2.5-8B-A1B is the new flagship of the family of models designed to run directly on-device, without routing through a remote server. Liquid AI uploaded the weights to Hugging Face on May 28, 2026, for a language model capable of running on an iPhone at roughly 30 tokens per second while staying under 6 GB of memory.

## Architecture

The architecture has 24 layers, of which 18 are double-gated short-convolution blocks based on the lab's proprietary LIV design, and 6 are GQA layers (Grouped Query Attention, an efficient form of attention that shares keys across multiple heads to reduce memory consumption). This blend of convolutions and attention is Liquid AI's technical signature. The convolutional blocks handle local dependencies at low computational cost, while the few attention layers take care of long-range relationships in the text.

## Parameters and MoE Design

8B indicates the total parameters (8.3 billion to be precise), while A1B stands for "active 1B", meaning the number of parameters actually computed at each pass. The model has 8.3B total parameters, 1.5B active per token (MoE with 32 experts, 4 active).

## Additional Features

The context length is 131,072 tokens (128K), and the vocabulary was doubled, growing from 65,536 to 128,000 tokens. LFM2.5-8B-A1B is a reasoning-only model, producing an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

The model weights are available openly on Hugging Face as part of Liquid AI's open-weight release.

content.text:
Ouro tops out at 2.6B, so looped-depth has no in-band representative — that mechanism is off the table at 7–15B. Here's the revised set, all decoder-only next-token predictors.

## Revised shortlist — autoregressive only

| Model | Params | Released | Sequence-mixing mechanism | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ministral 3 14B** (Mistral) | 14B dense | Dec 2025 | Plain dense transformer — the control | Apache-2.0 |
| **Falcon-H1R-7B** (TII) | 7.6B dense | 5 Jan 2026 | Attention + Mamba-2 SSM interleaved | TII licence |
| **ZAYA1-8B** (Zyphra) | 8.4B / **760M active** | 6 May 2026 | MoE + Compressed Convolutional Attention | Apache-2.0 |
| **LFM2.5-8B-A1B** (Liquid AI) | 8.3B / 1.5B active | 28 May 2026 | 18 short-conv LIV + 6 GQA layers, MoE 32/4 | LFM licence |
| **Gemma 4 12B** (Google) | 12B dense | 3 Jun 2026 | Dense, encoder-free unified multimodal | Apache-2.0 |

**ZAYA1-8B replaces the diffusion model.** The two MoEs aren't redundant — they're a controlled contrast. Same rough size, same sparse routing, completely different mixers: ZAYA1 does attention in a compressed latent space with convolutional preconditioners, LFM2.5 does short convolutions with only 6 attention layers out of 24. And their sparsity ratios differ sharply (11:1 vs 5.5:1), so parameter-counting code has to get both right.

## Why each is autoregressive

Worth being explicit, since three of these have mechanisms that superficially look non-AR:

- **Mamba-2 layers** (Falcon-H1R) are causal recurrences — if anything *more* strictly sequential than attention.
- **Short convolutions** (LFM2.5) are causal convolutions; they see only the left context.
- **MoE routing** (ZAYA1, LFM2.5) changes *which weights* compute a token, never the order tokens are produced in.
- **Encoder-free multimodality** (Gemma 4 12B) changes what goes into the context, not how text comes out — images are input, generation is still next-token.

None of these touch the training objective. All five are next-token prediction, left to right.

## Two practical catches for your beam-search work

**LFM2.5-8B-A1B is reasoning-only** — it always emits an explicit chain of thought before its answer. For notebooks 01/02 that changes what "the most probable 10-token continuation" even means: you'd be beam-searching over reasoning preamble, not the answer. Either budget for it in `num_tokens_to_generate` or treat it as a known asymmetry in the write-up.

**Ministral 3 ships base / instruct / reasoning variants.** Take the **base** one — instruct-tuned weights distort next-token probabilities with chat-template priors, which is exactly the thing your greedy-vs-beam gain measurement is trying to read.

## Unchanged from before

Feasibility splits the same way: header-level work via `raw_tensors()` works for all five; full `torch` loads for activations work for none (7–15B is 28–60 GB at float32, 14–30 GB at bf16, against 15.61 GB). Smaller siblings exist for four of the five — Ministral 3 3B, Falcon-H1-1.5B, LFM2-1.2B (already in notebook 02), Gemma 4 E2B/E4B. **ZAYA1-8B has no smaller sibling**, so it's weight-level only.

Ministral 3 14B is the weakest on recency (Dec 2025). If you'd rather have a 2026 date than a clean dense control, **Qwen3.5-9B** swaps in — but your own measurement found it carries `linear_attn.A_log` / `dt_bias`, so it's a gated-DeltaNet hybrid, doubling up on Falcon-H1R's family rather than giving you a plain baseline. I'd keep Ministral for that reason.

Same offer as before: I can run `scripts/compare_architectures.py` against these five to confirm the mechanism claims from actual tensor names before you commit, and write it up as `docs/candidate-models-7b-15b-2026.md`.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Qwen3.5-9B:

## Architecture

Qwen3.5-9B uses a hybrid architecture combining Gated Delta Networks and Gated Attention in an 8×(3×DeltaNet→FFN→1×Attention→FFN) pattern. More specifically, the architecture is a hybrid with roughly 75% Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers and 25% full softmax attention with GQA/RoPE.

Gated DeltaNet is O(n) and does not grow the KV cache at all - it maintains a fixed-size state vector that gets updated with a delta rule plus exponential gating.

## Open Weights & Licensing

All open-weight under Apache 2.0 except the hosted-only Plus tier. More specifically, Qwen3.5-9B is Alibaba Cloud's efficient multimodal foundation model with 9B parameters, released February 2026.

Clear result: **of the four labs you named, only Qwen ships a native model in 7–15B.** The others are frontier-scale MoE houses now.

## What each lab actually has in-band

| Lab | Smallest native model | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Qwen** | **Qwen3.5-9B** — 9B, Apache-2.0, Feb 2026 | ✅ In band |
| **DeepSeek** | DeepSeek-V4-Flash — 284B / 13B active | ❌ Only 7–15B offerings are R1-Distill 7B/8B/14B |
| **Moonshot / Kimi** | Kimi Linear — 48B / 3B active (K3 is 2.8T / 104B) | ❌ 48B total |
| **MiniMax** | MiniMax-M2.5 — 230B / 8B active (M3 is 428B / 23B) | ❌ 230B total |

Two traps worth naming explicitly:

**The DeepSeek distills are not DeepSeek architecture.** `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B` and `-Llama-8B` are Qwen2.5 and Llama3 backbones fine-tuned on R1-generated reasoning traces. Loading one and inspecting its tensors tells you about Qwen2.5, not about DeepSeek. For your weight-layout work they're actively misleading.

**Active parameters don't govern memory.** Kimi Linear at "3B active" and MiniMax-M2.5 at "8B active" look in-band, but you must hold *all* experts resident — 48B and 230B total. That's 96 GB and 460 GB at bf16.

## Revised shortlist

Qwen3.5-9B goes in. Its architecture is more interesting than your existing doc's correction suggested: an 8×(3× Gated DeltaNet → FFN → 1× Gated Attention → FFN) pattern, so ~75% linear-attention layers. Gated DeltaNet keeps a fixed-size state updated by a delta rule plus exponential gating — no KV cache growth at all.

| Model | Params | Mechanism | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Qwen3.5-9B** | 9B dense | Gated DeltaNet (3:1) + gated attention | Apache-2.0 |
| **ZAYA1-8B** | 8.4B / 760M active | MoE + Compressed Convolutional Attention | Apache-2.0 |
| **LFM2.5-8B-A1B** | 8.3B / 1.5B active | 18 short-conv LIV + 6 GQA, MoE 32/4 | LFM licence |
| **Gemma 4 12B** | 12B dense | Dense, encoder-free multimodal | Apache-2.0 |
| **Ministral 3 14B** | 14B dense | Plain dense transformer — control | Apache-2.0 |

**Falcon-H1R-7B is a free sixth** if you want it — you already have its tensor manifest, and Mamba-2 is a genuinely different fixed-state recurrence from Gated DeltaNet, so pairing it with Qwen3.5-9B is a real contrast rather than a duplicate. That's a better use of the slot than what your existing doc's correction implied, now that the layer pattern is known.

All six are decoder-only next-token predictors.

## You can still study DeepSeek, Kimi and MiniMax — at header level

This is the part worth acting on. `scripts/compare_architectures.py` reads safetensors headers straight from the Hub without downloading, which is how you got the four-model comparison for ~60 GB of weights you never pulled. **Total parameter count is irrelevant to that path.** So DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B), Kimi Linear (48B, Kimi Delta Attention) and MiniMax-M2.5 (230B) can all join a weight-layout comparison on equal terms — you'd get tensor names, shapes, expert counts, and the actual attention mechanism per layer, at zero RAM cost.

That splits your work cleanly in two:

- **Runnable shortlist** (the five above) — beam search, quantised inference, activation work via smaller siblings.
- **Header-only architecture survey** — add DeepSeek, Kimi, MiniMax, and compare MSA vs KDA vs Gated DeltaNet vs CCA vs Mamba-2 as tensor layouts. Five distinct linear/sparse attention formulations from five labs is a stronger finding than anything the runnable set alone gives you.

Want me to run `compare_architectures.py` across both groups and write it up? Given the Qwen3.5-9B mislabel already caught once in this project, confirming these from tensor names before committing seems worth the hour.

"""Research project package.

Every model used by this project lives in ``<project>/models``. Importing this
package enforces that by pointing the Hugging Face cache at
``research.paths.MODELS``, so nothing is downloaded to — or read from — the
default profile cache under the user profile.

The pin is **forced, not a default**: a stray ``HF_HUB_CACHE`` in the ambient
environment must not be able to redirect weights back outside the project.

It must run before ``huggingface_hub`` is imported, because that module reads
the cache location once at import time. In practice: import ``research`` (or
anything from it) before ``transformers`` or ``huggingface_hub``. If that order
is violated, :func:`research.models.load` raises rather than silently reading
from the wrong cache.
"""

import os

from .paths import MODELS

__version__ = "0.1.0"

MODELS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Forced assignment, not setdefault - see module docstring.
os.environ["HF_HUB_CACHE"] = str(MODELS)
os.environ["TRANSFORMERS_CACHE"] = str(MODELS)  # legacy name, still read by older code

# Symlink creation fails here, which aborts a download *after* the weights have
# transferred, so tell huggingface_hub to copy instead. Measured on this machine:
# on NTFS os.symlink raises WinError 1314 ("A required privilege is not held by
# the client") because Windows gates symlinks behind elevation or Developer Mode;
# on the exFAT volume this project used to live on it raised WinError 1
# ("Incorrect function") because the filesystem has no symlink support at all.
# Either way the fix is the same. Note this is a different variable from
# HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS_WARNING, which only silences the message and does not

os.environ["HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS"] = "1"
os.environ["HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS_WARNING"] = "1"

Verified against the live config rather than the docs:

## Where downloads land

```
C:\research\models          <- what all the code sees (paths.MODELS)
   └─ junction to →  D:\research\models      <- where the bytes physically are
```

`research/__init__.py` **forces** `HF_HUB_CACHE` (and the legacy `TRANSFORMERS_CACHE`) to `paths.MODELS` at import time — a forced assignment, not a default, so a stray env var can't redirect it. Confirmed live: `huggingface_hub`'s own `HF_HUB_CACHE` constant reads `C:\research\models`, and that resolves to `D:\research\models`.

The catch is ordering: `huggingface_hub` reads the cache location **once, at import**. So `import research` must come before `transformers` / `huggingface_hub`, or the pin misses. `models.load()` passes `cache_dir` explicitly as a second line of defence and raises if the order was violated.

## Layout on disk

```
models--Qwen--Qwen3.5-9B/
  refs/main                          <- the commit hash
  snapshots/<commit>/…               <- the actual files
  blobs/                             <- empty
```

`blobs/` is empty because `HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS=1` — normally the real file sits in `blobs/` and `snapshots/` symlinks to it, but symlinks fail on this machine (`WinError 1314`), so files are copied straight into `snapshots/`.

## What's there now — 26 GB

| Repo | Size |
|---|---|
| `google--gemma-4-E4B` | 16.02 GB |
| `Qwen--Qwen3-1.7B` | 4.08 GB |
| `tiiuae--Falcon-H1-1.5B-Instruct` | 3.11 GB |
| `LiquidAI--LFM2-1.2B` | 2.35 GB |
| `gpt2` | 0.55 GB |
| `Qwen--Qwen3.5-9B` | ~0 GB |
| `tiiuae--Falcon-H1R-7B` | ~0 GB |

The last two are the interesting ones for your question: those are what `compare_architectures.py` leaves behind. It fetches only `model.safetensors.index.json` (~80 KB) to read tensor names and shapes — **no weights at all**. That's why the header-only survey of DeepSeek/Kimi/MiniMax I suggested costs essentially nothing on disk.

## Space

- **D: 569 GB free** — plenty. The five shortlisted models at bf16 would be roughly 105 GB.
- C: 61 GB free, and downloads don't touch it.

One exception: `models.load(..., stage=True)` copies a single model to `C:\research\.model-cache\` (currently empty) for faster repeated loads. Single slot — staging a second model wipes the first, so it can't grow into a duplicate of `models/`.

So: header survey is free, and full downloads are safe on space. Want me to run the header comparison across the shortlist plus DeepSeek/Kimi/MiniMax now?

"""Compare how different architectures lay out their weights.

Reads safetensors headers straight from the Hub, so nothing is downloaded: the
header carries every tensor name, shape and dtype, which is all a layout
comparison needs. Downloading these four models in full would be ~60 GB for
information that is a few hundred KB.

Writes a per-model tensor manifest to results/<model>/ and a combined table to
results/architecture-comparison.csv.

    uv run python scripts/compare_architectures.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from collections import Counter

import research  # noqa: F401  - pins the HF cache to C:/research/models
import pandas as pd
from huggingface_hub import get_safetensors_metadata

from research import paths

MODELS = {
    "tiiuae/Falcon-H1R-7B": "attention + Mamba-2 SSM",
    "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B": "attention + linear attention",
    "google/gemma-4-E4B": "attention + per-layer embeddings",
    "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-8B-A1B": "attention + short conv + sparse MoE",
}

# Patterns taken from tensor names actually observed in these repos, not
# guessed. Guessed patterns matched everything and were useless.
MECHANISMS = {
    "softmax attention": r"self_attn\.",
    "state-space / linear attn": r"\bA_log\b|\bdt_bias\b",
    "sparse MoE": r"\.experts\.|expert_bias",
    "short convolution": r"conv1d|\.conv\.conv\.",
    "per-layer embedding / altup": r"altup|per_layer|laurel",
    "vision tower": r"\bvisual\b|vision_tower",
    "audio tower": r"audio_tower",
    "QAT ranges": r"input_max|output_max",
}

# Which part of the network a tensor belongs to.
COMPONENTS = {
    "vision": r"\bvisual\b|vision_tower",
    "audio": r"audio_tower",
}


def role(name: str) -> str:
    """Collapse block indices so 'layers.0.q' and 'layers.7.q' share a role."""
    return re.sub(r"\.\d+\.", ".N.", name)


def component(name: str) -> str:
    for label, pattern in COMPONENTS.items():
        if re.search(pattern, name):
            return label

Deletion is done — and note the four existing manifests in `results/` survived, since I only cleared `models/`.

## Updated list, two tiers

**Tier 1 — runnable in-band (7–15B, autoregressive)**

| Repo id | Params | Sequence mixing | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` | 9B | Gated DeltaNet 3:1 + gated attention | Apache-2.0 |
| `Zyphra/Zaya1-8B` | 8.4B / 760M active | MoE + Compressed Convolutional Attention | Apache-2.0 |
| `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-8B-A1B` | 8.3B / 1.5B active | 18 short-conv LIV + 6 GQA, MoE 32/4 | LFM |
| `google/gemma-4-12B` | 12B | Dense, encoder-free multimodal | Apache-2.0 |
| `tiiuae/Falcon-H1R-7B` | 7.6B | Attention + Mamba-2 SSM | TII |
| Ministral 3 14B | 14B | Plain dense — control | Apache-2.0 |

**Tier 2 — DeepSeek and Kimi, header-only**

| Repo id | Params | Sequence mixing |
|---|---|---|
| `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash` | 284B / 13B active | Compressed Sparse Attention + Heavily Compressed Attention |
| `moonshotai/Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Base` | 48B / 3B active | Kimi Delta Attention |

Both ids verified against Hugging Face. Neither can go in Tier 1 at any quantisation — 284B and 48B *total* must be resident to load, regardless of active count — but at header level their size is irrelevant, and each costs ~80 KB.

The payoff for adding them is real: with DeepSeek and Kimi in, the survey covers **six distinct sequence-mixing formulations** — CSA/HCA, KDA, Gated DeltaNet, CCA, Mamba-2, and short convolutions. That's a considerably stronger finding than the runnable set alone supports, and it's the comparison the project's tooling is actually built for.

## Two practical notes

**`DeepSeek-V4-Flash` ships in fp8.** Your manifests so far have been F32/BF16, so `get_safetensors_metadata` will report a dtype your tensor-manifest code hasn't seen. Worth watching when the script runs.

**Adding a model means adding a mechanism pattern too.** `scripts/compare_architectures.py` has a `MECHANISMS` dict whose comment records a lesson you already learned — *"Patterns taken from tensor names actually observed in these repos, not guessed. Guessed patterns matched everything and were useless."* CSA/HCA, KDA and CCA all need new patterns, and by that rule they have to be written **after** dumping the tensor names, not before.

So the sequence is: add the eight ids to `MODELS`, run once to get raw names, then write the patterns from what's actually there, then re-run.

Want me to do that now? It re-creates small header-only entries in the freshly-emptied `models/` (~80 KB each, no weights), and I'd write the result up as `docs/candidate-models-7b-15b-2026.md`. I'd also need to confirm the Ministral 3 14B repo id — it's the one on the list I haven't verified.

Short answer: **no — none of the eight can be loaded into torch on this machine.** Here's the arithmetic, measured against live memory rather than the doc.

Right now: **15.61 GiB total, 3.53 GiB available** (77.4% used). Your own `local-llm-on-snapdragon-x.md` puts the realistic budget at ~9 GB with most apps closed.

| Model | Params | float32 | bfloat16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Falcon-H1R-7B | 7.6B | 30.4 GB | **15.2 GB** |
| LFM2.5-8B-A1B | 8.3B | 33.2 GB | 16.6 GB |
| Zaya1-8B | 8.4B | 33.6 GB | 16.8 GB |
| Qwen3.5-9B | 9.0B | 36.0 GB | 18.0 GB |
| gemma-4-12B | 12B | 48.0 GB | 24.0 GB |
| Ministral 3 14B | 14B | 56.0 GB | 28.0 GB |
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B | 48B | 192 GB | 96 GB |
| DeepSeek-V4-Flash | 284B | — | 284 GB (native fp8) |

Even the smallest at bfloat16 needs 15.2 GB against 15.61 GB *total* — before Windows. At a 9 GB budget your ceiling is ~2.2B params at fp32 or ~4.5B at bf16. Nothing here is close.

**Active parameters don't help.** Zaya1's 760M and Kimi Linear's 3B active are compute figures — all experts must be resident to route.

## Why "not worried about speed" doesn't rescue it

This is the part I'd push back on. You have a **90 GiB pagefile**, so a 28 GB allocation won't fail cleanly with an OOM — it will *succeed* and then thrash. Every forward pass page-faults against disk, the working set never fits, and the machine typically goes unresponsive rather than slow. That's not a long wait you can leave running; it's a lockup plus sustained write load on the SSD. It's a different failure mode from "slow", which is why I'd not treat speed-tolerance as consent here.

Worth knowing: **`models.load()` has no size guard.** It calls `from_pretrained` directly, so nothing in the codebase stops the attempt. The only guard that exists is `params_from_headers()` + `FLOAT32_BUDGET_GIB = 9.0` in notebook 02 — that pattern is doing real work and should front any load of these.

## The other sense of "safely"

Several of these need **`trust_remote_code=True`** — Kimi Linear ships its own `modeling_kimi.py`, and ZAYA1's CCA, LFM2.5's LIV blocks and Falcon-H1R's Mamba-2 layers may too, depending on what transformers 5.15.1 supports natively. That executes arbitrary Python from the Hub at load time. Distinct risk from memory, and worth deciding deliberately rather than by passing a flag to silence an error.

## What is safe, and works on all eight

**Header reads.** `get_safetensors_metadata()` / `models.raw_tensors()` / `read_tensor()` parse the safetensors header — no code execution, nothing materialised, size irrelevant. DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B costs the same ~80 KB as gpt2. This is exactly the path `compare_architectures.py` already uses, and it's how you got manifests for ~60 GB of weights you never pulled.

**For actual torch loads**, the small siblings are the only option — and they fit comfortably:

| Sibling | fp32 | Fits in 9 GB? |
|---|---|---|
| gpt2 | 0.5 GB | ✅ |
| LiquidAI/LFM2-1.2B | 4.8 GB | ✅ |
| tiiuae/Falcon-H1-1.5B-Instruct | 6.0 GB | ✅ |
| Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B | 6.8 GB | ✅ |

That's precisely the four notebook 02 already declares — the notebook is built around this constraint, and I'd keep that split rather than fight it. Note ZAYA1-8B has no small sibling, so it stays header-only.

One untested possibility: `bitsandbytes==0.50.1` does resolve for win_arm64 here. But resolving isn't running — bnb's CPU int4/int8 backends are the shakiest part of that library, and I'd not build a plan on it without testing first.

So the realistic shape of the work: **header-level architecture survey across all eight** (safe, free, and the stronger finding anyway), **torch/activation work on the four small siblings**. Want me to run the survey on that basis?

    sequence every step, which is the constraint this implementation is built to.

    # without it `del outputs` would free nothing at all.
    logits = outputs.logits[:, -1, :].to(torch.float32).clone()

Everything is staged and verified except the weights. Status:

**Built:** `notebooks/03-beam-search-teddy-bear.ipynb` — 27 cells, ruff-clean, all 27 cells carry ids.

I made it a new notebook rather than editing 02, because notebook 02 *is* the "four architectures, width 10, declarative stem" experiment — overwriting its config would destroy that. Notebook 03 follows the project's self-sufficiency rule: the setup cell and all three `beam-search-implementation` cells are copied **verbatim** from 02, not imported.

**Verified:** `tests/test_beam.py` globs `notebooks/*.ipynb`, so it picked up notebook 03 automatically — 127 tests pass, including the new `[03-beam-search-teddy-bear]` parametrisations. That confirms the copied implementation genuinely executes and behaves identically, rather than just looking right.

**Config:** `CONFIG` is byte-identical to notebooks 01/02 (width 10, 10 tokens, top-10 per beam, seed 0), so the only variables are the prompt and the models. `PROMPT = "Write a funny story about a teddy bear."`

**Two departures from project defaults, both documented in the notebook:**

- `DTYPE = torch.bfloat16` — both repos are stored BF16 upstream, so this means *zero dtype conversion at load* and the tensors stay memory-mapped. Requesting float32 would force conversion into anonymous memory, which here can only go to the pagefile.
- `BF16_BUDGET_GIB = 16.0`, raised from notebook 02's `9.0`. The guard is kept rather than deleted, and now prints an explicit warning when a model exceeds physical RAM — so the run reports what it's doing instead of pretending the load is routine. Your decision is recorded in the cell comment with the numbers behind it.

**Downloading:** 4.4 GB of ~32 GB. Falcon-H1R-7B first, LFM2.5-8B-A1B after.

Two things I'll flag now rather than after the fact:

**Runtime is genuinely unknown.** The search is 10 batched forward passes for the beam plus 10 for greedy, but each pass touches weights that don't fit in RAM. Falcon-H1R is dense — all 14.13 GiB hot every pass. LFM2.5 is MoE with ~1.5B active, so mmap may only fault in the routed experts, which could make the *larger* model faster. I'll time the first forward pass and give you a real ETA before committing to the full sweep.

**10 tokens is very short for a "story."** It's what makes this comparable to notebooks 01/02, so I've kept it. If you'd rather see actual prose, say the word and I'll raise `num_tokens_to_generate` — but on these models each extra token is expensive, so it's worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering it at hour three.

I'll pick this up when the download finishes.

Two consequences worth stating before I change it, because they compound:

**Cost is quadratic, not linear.** There's no KV cache — every step recomputes the whole sequence from scratch. Going 10 → 100 tokens is ~40× the work, not 10×: the step count rises 10× *and* the average sequence length rises ~5×. On weights that don't fit in RAM, that multiplies against disk I/O too.

**`CONFIG` stops being identical to notebooks 01/02**, so this run is no longer directly comparable to them on sequence probability. That's fine — it's the right call for actual prose — but I'll record it in the notebook rather than let it silently break the comparison.

Also: I'll put "100 tokens" in the prompt as you asked, though models generally steer better on *words* than tokens. Flagging it; using tokens since that's what you specified.

"""Time one load + two forward passes on Falcon-H1R-7B at bf16, to get a real ETA."""
import research  # pins HF cache - must be first
import time

import psutil
import torch

from research import models

MODEL_ID = "tiiuae/Falcon-H1R-7B"
PROMPT = "Write a funny story about a teddy bear in about 100 tokens."
BEAM_WIDTH = 10


def rss():
    return psutil.Process().memory_info().rss / 2**30


def free():
    return psutil.virtual_memory().available / 2**30


print(f"before load: rss {rss():.2f} GiB, system free {free():.2f} GiB", flush=True)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
model, tok = models.load(MODEL_ID, torch.bfloat16)
load_s = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"LOAD {load_s:.0f}s  rss {rss():.2f} GiB  free {free():.2f} GiB", flush=True)

ids = tok(PROMPT, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
n_prompt = ids.shape[1]
print(f"prompt tokens: {n_prompt}", flush=True)
print(f"blocks: {len(models.block_names(model))}  vocab: {model.config.vocab_size}", flush=True)


@torch.inference_mode()
def one_pass(seq_len, batch):
    """One batched forward pass at a given sequence length, as the search does it."""
    x = ids[:, :1].repeat(batch, seq_len)[:, :seq_len]
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = model(input_ids=x, attention_mask=torch.ones_like(x), use_cache=False)
    _ = out.logits[:, -1, :].to(torch.float32).clone()
    del out
    return time.perf_counter() - t


# Warm pass first: the very first forward faults in weights and is not typical.
warm = one_pass(n_prompt, BEAM_WIDTH)
print(f"PASS warm      seq={n_prompt:3d} batch={BEAM_WIDTH}  {warm:7.1f}s  free {free():.2f} GiB", flush=True)

short = one_pass(n_prompt, BEAM_WIDTH)
print(f"PASS short     seq={n_prompt:3d} batch={BEAM_WIDTH}  {short:7.1f}s", flush=True)

long_len = n_prompt + 100
long = one_pass(long_len, BEAM_WIDTH)
print(f"PASS long      seq={long_len:3d} batch={BEAM_WIDTH}  {long:7.1f}s", flush=True)

# The search does 100 steps, sequence growing from n_prompt to n_prompt+100.
# Interpolate per-step cost linearly in sequence length between the two measurements.
slope = (long - short) / (long_len - n_prompt)
beam_total = sum(short + slope * i for i in range(100))
greedy_total = beam_total / BEAM_WIDTH * 1.0  # batch 1; roughly linear in batch here
print(f"\nESTIMATE for 100 tokens, width {BEAM_WIDTH}:", flush=True)
print(f"  beam   ~{beam_total/60:7.1f} min", flush=True)
print(f"  greedy ~{greedy_total/60:7.1f} min (batch 1, optimistic)", flush=True)
print(f"  total  ~{(beam_total+greedy_total)/3600:7.2f} h  for this model alone", flush=True)
print("PROBE DONE", flush=True)

The forward passes are where pages actually fault in, so that's the number that matters.

"""Escalating timing probe: cheap passes first, hard time budget, incremental output.

Run conditions matter for this measurement, so they are printed up front.
"""
import research  # pins HF cache - must be first
import time

import psutil
import torch

from research import models

MODEL_ID = "tiiuae/Falcon-H1R-7B"
PROMPT = "Write a funny story about a teddy bear in about 100 tokens."
BUDGET_S = 1500          # stop escalating past ~25 min total
started = time.perf_counter()


def free():
    return psutil.virtual_memory().available / 2**30


def rss():
    return psutil.Process().memory_info().rss / 2**30


def elapsed():
    return time.perf_counter() - started


print(f"conditions: free {free():.2f} GiB of "
      f"{psutil.virtual_memory().total / 2**30:.2f}, "
      f"cpu {psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1):.0f}%", flush=True)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
model, tok = models.load(MODEL_ID, torch.bfloat16)
print(f"LOAD {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f}s  rss {rss():.2f} GiB  free {free():.2f} GiB",
      flush=True)

ids = tok(PROMPT, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
n_prompt = ids.shape[1]
print(f"prompt {n_prompt} tokens | blocks {len(models.block_names(model))} "
      f"| vocab {model.config.vocab_size}", flush=True)


@torch.inference_mode()
def one_pass(seq_len, batch):
    x = ids[:, :1].repeat(batch, seq_len)
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = model(input_ids=x, attention_mask=torch.ones_like(x), use_cache=False)
    _ = out.logits[:, -1, :].to(torch.float32).clone()
    del out
    return time.perf_counter() - t


# Escalate cheapest-first. Each entry is (seq_len, batch, label).
PLAN = [
    (n_prompt, 1, "cold  b1  short"),   # first pass also faults the weights in
    (n_prompt, 1, "warm  b1  short"),   # the one to trust for b1
    (n_prompt + 100, 1, "warm  b1  long"),
    (n_prompt, 10, "warm  b10 short"),
    (n_prompt + 100, 10, "warm  b10 long"),
]

timings = {}
for seq_len, batch, label in PLAN:
    if elapsed() > BUDGET_S:
        print(f"BUDGET reached at {elapsed()/60:.1f} min; skipping '{label}' and the rest",
              flush=True)
        break
    took = one_pass(seq_len, batch)
    timings[(seq_len, batch)] = took
    print(f"PASS {label:16s} seq={seq_len:3d} batch={batch:2d}  {took:8.1f}s  "
          f"rss {rss():5.2f} GiB  free {free():5.2f} GiB  [t+{elapsed()/60:.1f}m]",
          flush=True)

print(f"\n--- extrapolation (100 tokens, width 10) ---", flush=True)
short10 = timings.get((n_prompt, 10))
long10 = timings.get((n_prompt + 100, 10))
if short10 and long10:
    slope = (long10 - short10) / 100
    beam = sum(short10 + slope * i for i in range(100))
    print(f"beam   ~{beam/3600:6.2f} h", flush=True)
    short1 = timings.get((n_prompt, 1))
    long1 = timings.get((n_prompt + 100, 1))
    if short1 and long1:
        slope1 = (long1 - short1) / 100
        greedy = sum(short1 + slope1 * i for i in range(100))
        print(f"greedy ~{greedy/3600:6.2f} h", flush=True)
        print(f"TOTAL  ~{(beam+greedy)/3600:6.2f} h for {MODEL_ID} alone", flush=True)
else:
    print("not enough batch-10 timings inside the budget to extrapolate", flush=True)
    for (s, b), t in timings.items():
        print(f"  measured seq={s} batch={b}: {t:.1f}s", flush=True)
print("PROBE2 DONE", flush=True)

content.text:
The probe was stopped, but it captured the two measurements that settle the question:

```
LOAD                6s   rss 0.32 GiB   free 6.34 GiB
PASS cold  b1 seq=17    374.5s   rss 8.10 GiB   free 0.17 GiB
PASS warm  b1 seq=17    376.6s   rss 8.56 GiB   free 0.22 GiB
```

## The decisive fact: warm ≈ cold

376.6s vs 374.5s. **Caching bought nothing — 0.6% difference.** RSS climbed to 8.56 GiB and free RAM collapsed to **0.17 GiB**.

That resolves the caveat I raised. Conditions this time were genuinely better — 6.2 GiB free at start instead of 3.2, no download competing for the disk — and it made no material difference. The problem isn't contention or a cold cache. 14.13 GiB of weights simply cannot be held in a machine that can spare ~8.5 GiB, so every pass evicts and re-reads the model in full. More headroom wouldn't fix it either.

The arithmetic confirms I/O is the bottleneck, not compute: batch=1 at seq=17 is ~2.6×10¹¹ FLOP in 376s — **0.7 GFLOPS**, roughly two orders of magnitude below what this CPU can do. Meanwhile 14.13 GiB ÷ 376s ≈ **38 MB/s**, which matches your own recorded D: read speed almost exactly (105.7s for Qwen3-1.7B's 3.9 GB ≈ 37 MB/s).

## What that means for the run

Since cost is dominated by streaming weights rather than arithmetic, batch=10 likely costs *little more* than batch=1 — the weights are read once per pass and applied to all 10 beams.

| | Optimistic (I/O-bound, likely) | Pessimistic (cost scales with batch) |
|---|---|---|
| Falcon-H1R-7B, beam + greedy | ~21 hours | ~8 days |
| Both models | **~2–3 days** | ~2 weeks |

I want to be clear that the optimistic column is an *inference* from the FLOPS analysis, not a measurement — the probe was stopped before reaching the batch=10 passes that would have pinned it down.

Either way, the machine sits near 0.2 GiB free throughout. That's not "slow in the background"; it's largely unusable for anything else for days.

## My recommendation

Switch to the small siblings. This isn't the modest trade-off it looked like earlier — the bottleneck *disappears* rather than shrinking. `Falcon-H1-1.5B-Instruct` at float32 is 6.0 GiB and `LFM2-1.2B` is 4.8 GiB, so both stay fully resident, no streaming, and the run becomes compute-bound. Expect roughly **30–60 minutes total** instead of 2–3 days, on the same two architecture families, with the full 100-token teddy-bear prompt and width 10 intact.

The 7–8B weights stay on disk either way, so nothing is wasted — and the header-level architecture survey I proposed earlier still works on them at full size regardless of RAM.

If you'd rather have the 7–8B numbers, I'll run it — say the word and I'll launch it in the background with per-step progress logging so you can watch it advance and kill it at any point. But I'd rather you choose that knowing it's days of a saturated machine, not hours.
